1118 CHAPTER 27 Peripheral Nerves and Skeletal Muscles
Pathogenesis
Dermatomyositis includes a group of inflammatory myopathies
that are characterized by dermatomyositis-specific antibodies
(DMSAs) and prominent type I interferon (IFN)-signaling pathway activation. The DMSAs are associated with distinctive clinical
and histopathologic features, discussed later. The exact role of these
antibodies in the pathogenesis of the disease process is unknown. The
activation of type I IFN signaling is a consistent feature of dermatomyositis and some systemic autoimmune diseases, notably lupus
(Chapter 6). The presence of tubuloreticular inclusions in capillary
endothelial cells and the overexpression of myxovirus resistant protein A (MxA), an IFN-induced antiviral protein, are viewed as histopathologic markers of abnormal IFN signaling, but the role of IFN in
disease pathogenesis is not established. Vasculopathic changes are
common, including telangiectasias (dilated capillary loops) in the nail
folds, eyelids, and gums and dropout of capillary vessels in skeletal
muscle, that are responsible for at least some of the manifestations
of dermatomyositis. It is postulated that the accumulation of IFN-induced proteins in muscle and vascular cells has a toxic effect that is
responsible for at least some of the injury.
MORPHOLOGY
The classic feature of dermatomyositis is perifascicular atrophy, a term that
describes the preferential atrophy of fibers at the edge of muscle fascicles
(Fig. 27.9B). However, it is found in only about 50% of cases and is especially
associated with anti-TIF-g as well as anti-Mi-2 antibodies. Other common
findings include perimysial perivascular inflammatory cell infiltrates rich in T
lymphocytes, perifascicular necrosis of myofibers (especially in cases with
anti-Mi-2 antibodies), and microinfarcts (especially in cases with anti-NXP-2
antibodies). Deposition of C5b-9 (the membrane attack complex of complement) in capillaries in perifascicular areas is seen in a subset of cases and
thought to underlie dropout of capillaries. MxA expression in muscle cells and
the formation of tubuloreticular endothelial inclusions on electron microscopic studies are, as mentioned, a reflection of the IFN response.
Clinical Features
Muscle weakness is subacute in onset, symmetric, and often accompanied by myalgias. It typically affects the proximal muscles first. As a
result, tasks such as getting up from a chair and climbing steps become
increasingly difficult. Fine movements controlled by distal muscles are
affected only late in the disease. Associated myopathic changes on electrophysiologic studies and elevation in serum creatine kinase levels are
reflective of muscle damage. Various skin manifestations are seen in
dermatomyositis, but the most characteristic ones are a lilac-colored
discoloration of the upper eyelids associated with periorbital edema
(heliotrope rash) (Fig. 27.9A) and a scaling erythematous eruption or
dusky red patches over the knuckles, elbows, and knees (Gottron papules). Dysphagia resulting from involvement of oropharyngeal and
esophageal muscles occurs in one-third of the affected individuals.
The clinical features vary in individuals with different antibody profiles.
• Antibodies against TIF1-g (a signaling protein): These patients often
have prominent skin involvement, dysphagia, and a significant association with a diagnosis of cancer in those over the age of 38 years.
• Antibodies against Mi-2 (a nucleosome protein): These patients usually have high serum CK levels because of severe muscle involvement
with prominent necrosis.
• Antibodies against MDA5 (an IFN-induced cytosolic viral sensor):
These patients often have little or no muscle involvement clinically
and only mild changes on muscle biopsy. They fall into different
subgroups. Some of these patients have rapidly progressive interstitial lung disease associated with a poor prognosis, while others
have skin manifestations combined with joint involvement causing
arthralgias and a comparably favorable prognosis.
• Antibodies against NXP-2 (a nuclear matrix protein): These patients typically have weakness related to muscle involvement but
limited cutaneous involvement. Some develop dystrophic calcifications in superficial soft tissues referred to as calcinosis.
Dermatomyositis is the most common inflammatory myopathy
encountered in children. Juvenile patients are enriched in the group
with anti-NXP-2 antibodies.

shows perifascicular atrophy of muscle fibers and inflammation. ( Courtesy Dr. Dennis Burns, Department of
Pathology, University of Texas Southwestern Medical School, Dallas.)

Pathogenesis

Dermatomyositis includes a group of inflammatory myopathies that are characterized by dermatomyositis-specific antibodies (DMSAs) and prominent type I interferon (IFN)-signaling pathway activation. The DMSAs are associated with distinctive clinical and histopathologic features, discussed later. The exact role of these antibodies in the pathogenesis of the disease process is unknown. The activation of type I IFN signaling is a consistent feature of dermatomyositis and some systemic autoimmune diseases, notably lupus (Chapter 6). The presence of tubuloreticular inclusions in capillary endothelial cells and the overexpression of myxovirus resistant protein A (MxA), an IFN-induced antiviral protein, are viewed as histopathologic markers of abnormal IFN signaling, but the role of IFN in disease pathogenesis is not established. Vasculopathic changes are common, including telangiectasias (dilated capillary loops) in the nail folds, eyelids, and gums and dropout of capillary vessels in skeletal muscle, that are responsible for at least some of the manifestations of dermatomyositis. CHAPTER 27 Peripheral Nerves and Skeletal Muscles 1119
Antisynthetase Syndrome
Antisynthetase syndrome is a disease that involves muscle and
other tissues and is defined by the presence of serum antibodies
directed against aminoacyl transfer RNA synthetase. The most common and prototypical form is associated with anti-Jo-1 antibodies but
cases with other antisynthetase antibodies are described including
anti-PL-7, anti-PL-12, anti-EJ, and anti-Ha. Clinical manifestations of
antisynthetase syndrome include muscle disease (myositis with muscle
weakness and myalgias), interstitial lung disease, and arthritis. Other
rare features may include arthralgias, fever, Raynaud phenomenon,
and skin manifestations. The latter include changes described as “me-chanic’s hands”, hyperkeratotic, fissuring patches on the radial aspects
of the fingers and the ulnar aspect of the thumb. The histopathologic
features of the myositis often include perifascicular atrophy and necrosis that can mimic dermatomyositis but other cases may show more
random distribution of necrotic myofibers.
Immune-Mediated Necrotizing Myopathy
Immune-mediated necrotizing myopathy (IMNM) is characterized
by prominent muscle necrosis with high CK levels and rapidly
progressive weakness. Associated systemic manifestations like skin
changes, arthritis, and interstitial lung disease are seen only in a small
subset of patients. IMNM is associated with antibodies against the
ribonucleoprotein SRP or against-HMG-CoA reductase, an enzyme
involved in cholesterol synthesis. Patients with anti-SRP antibodies
usually have more severe disease, more often have dysphagia, and may
develop cardiac involvement. Muscle biopsies typically show prominent myofiber damage with randomly admixed necrotic and regenerating myofibers and a paucity of associated inflammatory infiltrates.
Anti-HMG-CoA reductase antibodies can be seen in patients with
prior exposure to statins but are also reported in statin-naïve patients.
Sporadic Inclusion Body Myositis
Sporadic inclusion body myositis (sIBM) is a disease of late adulthood that typically affects patients older than 50 years and is the most
common inflammatory myopathy in patients older than 65 years.
Most affected individuals present with slowly progressive muscle weakness that tends to be most severe in the quadriceps and the distal upper
extremity muscles. Dysphagia from esophageal and pharyngeal muscle
involvement is not uncommon. Laboratory studies usually show relatively mild creatine kinase level elevations reflecting a more smoldering
disease course. Antibodies to cytosolic 59-nucleotidase 1A (cN1A) have
been described in association with many cases of sIBM.
MORPHOLOGY
Sporadic inclusion body myositis is associated with a distinct set of biopsy
changes in typical and established cases. These include:
• Patchy, often endomysial mononuclear inflammatory cell infiltrates rich in
CD8⁺ T cells
• Focal invasion of normal appearing myofibers by inflammatory cells
• Increased sarcolemmal expression of major histocompatibility complex
class I antigens
• Abnormal cytoplasmic inclusions described as “rimmed vacuoles” (Fig. 27.10)
that contain abnormal lysosomal aggregates and protein aggregates
typically associated with neurodegenerative diseases, like beta-amyloid,
TDP-43, and ubiquitin
• On electron microscopy, distinctive filamentous aggregates often found in
abnormal lysosomal structures
• Endomysial fibrosis and fatty replacement, reflective of a chronic disease
course
Whether inclusion body myositis is indeed an inflammatory condition or a degenerative process with secondary inflammatory changes
remains an unresolved question. It has certain features in common
with other idiopathic inflammatory myopathies but also shares some
features with neurodegenerative diseases, such as the presence of abnormal protein aggregates in muscle cells. Furthermore, there are
several familial inclusion body myopathies that are also associated
with chronic myopathic changes and rimmed vacuoles. These usually
lack any associated inflammation—hence the designation inclusion
body “myopathy” rather than “myositis.” Patients with sporadic inclusion body myositis typically respond poorly to steroids and other
immunosuppressive drugs used in the treatment of other idiopathic
inflammatory myopathies.
Polymyositis
Polymyositis used to be the third inflammatory myopathy in the original triad besides dermatomyositis and inclusion body myositis but
cases that were historically classified as polymyositis would now be
regarded as immune-mediated necrotizing myopathy, antisynthetase
syndrome, or sporadic inclusion body myositis.
Toxic Myopathies and Myopathy With
Metabolic Changes
Medications, non-medicinal drug use, and hormonal changes can
result in muscle damage causing weakness and CK level elevations.
Different mechanisms are described:
1. Statins, fibrates, and high doses of alcohol are examples of agents that
can cause acute damage and necrosis of individual myofibers. In
severe cases, muscle breakdown can result in rhabdomyolysis and
associated complications such as acute renal failure. The risk for
direct statin toxicity increases with the statin dose, and age over 65
years, renal failure, hepatic failure, and hypothyroidism. Affected
patients typically improve with discontinuation of the offending
drug and supportive care.
Fig. 27.10 Inclusion body myositis, showing myofibers containing
rimmed vacuoles—inclusions with reddish granular rimming (arrows).
Modified Gömöri trichrome stain.

Antisynthetase Syndrome

Antisynthetase syndrome is a disease that involves muscle and other tissues and is defined by the presence of serum antibodies directed against aminoacyl transfer RNA synthetase. The most common and prototypical form is associated with anti-Jo-1 antibodies but cases with other antisynthetase antibodies are described including anti-PL-7, anti-PL-12, anti-EJ, and anti-Ha. Clinical manifestations of antisynthetase syndrome include muscle disease (myositis with muscle weakness and myalgias), interstitial lung disease, and arthritis. Other rare features may include arthralgias, fever, Raynaud phenomenon, and skin manifestations. The latter include changes described as “me-chanic’s hands”, hyperkeratotic, fissuring patches on the radial aspects of the fingers and the ulnar aspect of the thumb. The histopathologic features of the myositis often include perifascicular atrophy and necrosis that can mimic dermatomyositis but other cases may show more random distribution of necrotic myofibers.
Immune-Mediated Necrotizing Myopathy

Immune-mediated necrotizing myopathy (IMNM) is characterized by prominent muscle necrosis with high CK levels and rapidly progressive weakness. Associated systemic manifestations like skin changes, arthritis, and interstitial lung disease are seen only in a small subset of patients. IMNM is associated with antibodies against the ribonucleoprotein SRP or against-HMG-CoA reductase, an enzyme involved in cholesterol synthesis. Patients with anti-SRP antibodies usually have more severe disease, more often have dysphagia, and may develop cardiac involvement. Muscle biopsies typically show prominent myofiber damage with randomly admixed necrotic and regenerating myofibers and a paucity of associated inflammatory infiltrates. Anti-HMG-CoA reductase antibodies can be seen in patients with prior exposure to statins but are also reported in statin-naïve patients. Sporadic Inclusion Body Myositis Sporadic inclusion body myositis (sIBM) is a disease of late adulthood that typically affects patients older than 50 years and is the most common inflammatory myopathy in patients older than 65 years. Most affected individuals present with slowly progressive muscle weakness that tends to be most severe in the quadriceps and the distal upper extremity muscles. Dysphagia from esophageal and pharyngeal muscle involvement is not uncommon. Laboratory studies usually show relatively mild creatine kinase level elevations reflecting a more smoldering disease course. Antibodies to cytosolic 59-nucleotidase 1A (cN1A) have been described in association with many cases of sIBM. MORPHOLOGY Sporadic inclusion body myositis is associated with a distinct set of biopsy changes in typical and established cases. These include:
• Patchy, often endomysial mononuclear inflammatory cell infiltrates rich in CD8⁺ T cells
• Focal invasion of normal appearing myofibers by inflammatory cells
• Increased sarcolemmal expression of major histocompatibility complex class I antigens

• Abnormal cytoplasmic inclusions described as “rimmed vacuoles” (Fig. 27.10) that contain abnormal lysosomal aggregates and protein aggregates typically associated with neurodegenerative diseases, like beta-amyloid, TDP-43, and ubiquitin
• On electron microscopy, distinctive filamentous aggregates often found in abnormal lysosomal structures

• Endomysial fibrosis and fatty replacement, reflective of a chronic disease course Whether inclusion body myositis is indeed an inflammatory condition or a degenerative process with secondary inflammatory changes remains an unresolved question. It has certain features in common with other idiopathic inflammatory myopathies but also shares some features with neurodegenerative diseases, such as the presence of abnormal protein aggregates in muscle cells. Furthermore, there are several familial inclusion body myopathies that are also associated with chronic myopathic changes and rimmed vacuoles. These usually lack any associated inflammation—hence the designation inclusion body “myopathy” rather than “myositis.” Patients with sporadic inclusion body myositis typically respond poorly to steroids and other immunosuppressive drugs used in the treatment of other idiopathic inflammatory myopathies.
Polymyositis

Polymyositis used to be the third inflammatory myopathy in the original triad besides dermatomyositis and inclusion body myositis but cases that were historically classified as polymyositis would now be regarded as immune-mediated necrotizing myopathy, antisynthetase syndrome, or sporadic inclusion body myositis.
Toxic Myopathies and Myopathy With
Metabolic Changes

Medications, non-medicinal drug use, and hormonal changes can result in muscle damage causing weakness and CK level elevations. Different mechanisms are described: 1. Statins, fibrates, and high doses of alcohol are examples of agents that can cause acute damage and necrosis of individual myofibers. In severe cases, muscle breakdown can result in rhabdomyolysis and associated complications such as acute renal failure. The risk for direct statin toxicity increases with the statin dose, and age over 65 years, renal failure, hepatic failure, and hypothyroidism. Affected patients typically improve with discontinuation of the offending drug and supportive care.

2. Some medications like statins and immune checkpoint inhibitors can
trigger an immune-mediated myopathy. The distinction between
pure statin toxicity and IMNM in the context of statin exposure
(discussed earlier) is sometimes difficult to make at the time of
presentation.
3. Antiretrovirals like zidovudine can lead to mitochondrial damage
and a form of acquired mitochondrial myopathy (see below).
4. Medications that interfere with lysosomal function such as hydroxychlo-roquine and chloroquine can cause a myopathy of insidious onset that
mimics a lysosomal storage disease. The muscle tissue in such cases
shows myopathic changes including vacuolation that predominantly
affects type I fibers. Ultrastructural studies identify aggregates of
whorled, lamellar membranous structures. Cardiac muscle may also
be affected by these drugs and can exhibit similar pathologic changes.
5. Catabolic endogenous or exogenous corticosteroids can cause selective
atrophy of type II fibers and proximal muscle weakness. Critical illness myopathy, also known as myosin-deficient myopathy, is a
neuromuscular disorder seen in critically ill patients typically treated
in the ICU whose management includes corticosteroid therapy together with depolarizing neuromuscular blocking agents to allow
mechanical ventilation. In this setting, there may be relatively selective degradation of sarcomeric myosin thick filaments, producing
profound weakness that can complicate the clinical course, for example by interfering with weaning from mechanical ventilation.

myopathy presents most commonly as an acute or chronic proximal
muscle weakness that may precede other signs of hyperthyroidism.

characterized by swelling of the eyelids, edema of the conjunctiva,
and diplopia. Hypothyroidism can cause cramping or aching of
muscles. Movement and reflexes may be slowed. Findings in skeletal

Inherited Diseases of Skeletal Muscle
Inherited mutations causing defects in proteins needed for skeletal
muscle function are responsible for a diverse collection of disorders.
In some of these disorders, skeletal muscle is the main site of disease,
but in others multiple organs are involved. Of these, the heart is of
particular importance since cardiac involvement is common and
often life limiting. Channelopathies and metabolic myopathies are
also often the result of underlying mutations but will be discussed in
separate sections. Genetic neuromuscular diseases have been a major
target of efforts to introduce various forms of gene therapy, discussed
later.
Historically, inherited myopathies have been subdivided into
several broad categories based on inheritance pattern, anatomic pattern of muscle involvement, age of onset, clinical course, and underlying pathogenesis. Included in the group of inherited muscular
disorders are:
• Congenital myopathies (Table 27.3) typically present in infancy.
Some severe forms are associated with early lethality while others
may be associated with muscle defects that tend to be static and are
associated with a near-normal life span. Congenital myopathies are
often associated with distinct structural abnormalities of the muscle.
• Muscular dystrophies are characterized by progressive muscle damage that typically comes to attention after infancy (discussed later).
• Congenital muscular dystrophies tend to present in infancy and are
often associated with developmental abnormalities of the CNS as
well as progressive muscle damage. Congenital muscular dystrophies include two important groups:

3. Antiretrovirals like zidovudine can lead to mitochondrial damage and a form of acquired mitochondrial myopathy (see below). 4. Medications that interfere with lysosomal function such as hydroxychlo-roquine and chloroquine can cause a myopathy of insidious onset that mimics a lysosomal storage disease. The muscle tissue in such cases shows myopathic changes including vacuolation that predominantly affects type I fibers. Ultrastructural studies identify aggregates of whorled, lamellar membranous structures. Cardiac muscle may also be affected by these drugs and can exhibit similar pathologic changes. 5. Catabolic endogenous or exogenous corticosteroids can cause selective atrophy of type II fibers and proximal muscle weakness. Critical illness myopathy, also known as myosin-deficient myopathy, is a neuromuscular disorder seen in critically ill patients typically treated in the ICU whose management includes corticosteroid therapy together with depolarizing neuromuscular blocking agents to allow mechanical ventilation. In this setting, there may be relatively selective degradation of sarcomeric myosin thick filaments, producing profound weakness that can complicate the clinical course, for example by interfering with weaning from mechanical ventilation. 6. Thyroid dysfunction can lead to several types of myopathy. Thyrotoxic myopathy presents most commonly as an acute or chronic proximal muscle weakness that may precede other signs of hyperthyroidism. Such patients may also present with exophthalmic ophthalmoplegia, characterized by swelling of the eyelids, edema of the conjunctiva, and diplopia. Hypothyroidism can cause cramping or aching of muscles. Movement and reflexes may be slowed. Findings in skeletal

Inherited Diseases of Skeletal Muscle

Inherited mutations causing defects in proteins needed for skeletal muscle function are responsible for a diverse collection of disorders. In some of these disorders, skeletal muscle is the main site of disease, but in others multiple organs are involved. Of these, the heart is of particular importance since cardiac involvement is common and often life limiting. Channelopathies and metabolic myopathies are also often the result of underlying mutations but will be discussed in separate sections. Genetic neuromuscular diseases have been a major target of efforts to introduce various forms of gene therapy, discussed later.

• Congenital myopathies (Table 27.3) typically present in infancy. Some severe forms are associated with early lethality while others may be associated with muscle defects that tend to be static and are associated with a near-normal life span. Congenital myopathies are often associated with distinct structural abnormalities of the muscle.

• Congenital muscular dystrophies tend to present in infancy and are often associated with developmental abnormalities of the CNS as well as progressive muscle damage. Congenital muscular dystrophies include two important groups:

Muscular Dystrophies
Muscular dystrophies include many inherited disorders marked by
progressive skeletal muscle damage that typically manifest between
childhood and adulthood. As mentioned earlier, except for congenital
muscular dystrophies, these diseases do not present in infancy.
X-Linked Muscular Dystrophy With Dystrophin Mutation Including
Duchenne and Becker Muscular Dystrophy. The most common muscular dystrophies are X-linked and stem from mutations that disrupt the function of a large structural protein called dystrophin. As
a result, these diseases are sometimes referred to as dystrophinopathies.
The most common early-onset form is Duchenne muscular dystrophy.
It has an incidence of 1 per 3500 live male births and has a severe progressive phenotype. Becker muscular dystrophy is the second relatively
common dystrophinopathy; it is characterized by later disease onset
and a milder phenotype. Other rare dystrophinopathies may present
with isolated cardiomyopathy, asymptomatic elevations of CK levels,
or exercise intolerance because of myalgias and cramps. As with many
X-linked diseases, female carriers of dystrophin mutations may be
mildly symptomatic due to unfavorable X-chromosome inactivation.
Pathogenesis
Duchenne and Becker muscular dystrophies are caused by loss-of-function mutations in the dystrophin gene on the X chromosome.
Dystrophin is one of the largest human genes, spanning 2.3 million base
pairs and containing 79 exons. The encoded protein, dystrophin, is a
key component of the dystrophin glycoprotein complex (see Fig. 27.11).
This complex spans the plasma membrane and serves as a link between
the cytoskeleton inside the myofiber and the basement membrane outside of the cell. By doing so, dystrophin is thought to provide mechanical stability to the myofiber and its cell membrane during muscle contraction. Defects in the complex may lead to small membrane tears that
permit influx of calcium, triggering events that result in myofiber necrosis. In addition to its mechanical function, dystrophin may have a
role in signaling pathways; for example, its carboxy terminus interacts
with nitric oxide synthase, which generates nitric oxide (NO).
Identification and characterization of pathogenic dystrophin mutations has provided an explanation for some of the phenotypic variation
in patients with dystrophinopathies. Duchenne muscular dystrophy is
typically associated with deletions or frameshift mutations that result

MORPHOLOGY
The basic morphologic changes that muscular dystrophies elicit in skeletal
muscle tissue may differ in severity but are otherwise similar. The changes
in Duchenne muscular dystrophy serve as an example. This disease is
marked by chronic muscle injury that outpaces the capacity for repair
(Fig. 27.12). Muscle biopsies in young boys show ongoing damage in the
form of segmental myofiber necrosis and regeneration associated
with an admixture of atrophic myofibers. The fascicular architecture is
preserved during the earlier stages of the disease, and there is usually no
inflammation except for the presence of myophagocytosis. As the disease
progresses, muscle tissue is replaced by collagen and fat cells (“fatty replacement” or “fatty infiltration”). This remodeling distorts the fascicular
architecture of the muscle, which becomes markedly abnormal over time. At
later time points, the remaining myofibers show prominent variation in size
ranging from small atrophic fibers to large, hypertrophied fibers. Immunohistochemical studies for dystrophin can be used to document complete or
partial absence of dystrophin in Duchenne (Fig. 27.12B) and Becker muscular
dystrophy, respectively.

cular dystrophies are X-linked and stem from mutations that dis-
rupt the function of a large structural protein called dystrophin. As
a result, these diseases are sometimes referred to as dystrophinopathies.
The most common early-onset form is Duchenne muscular dystrophy.
It has an incidence of 1 per 3500 live male births and has a severe pro-
gressive phenotype. Becker muscular dystrophy is the second relatively
common dystrophinopathy; it is characterized by later disease onset
and a milder phenotype. Other rare dystrophinopathies may present
with isolated cardiomyopathy, asymptomatic elevations of CK levels,
or exercise intolerance because of myalgias and cramps. As with many
X-linked diseases, female carriers of dystrophin mutations may be
mildly symptomatic due to unfavorable X-chromosome inactivation.
Pathogenesis
Duchenne and Becker muscular dystrophies are caused by loss-of-
function mutations in the dystrophin gene on the X chromosome.
Dystrophin is one of the largest human genes, spanning 2.3 million base
pairs and containing 79 exons. The encoded protein, dystrophin, is a
key component of the dystrophin glycoprotein complex (see Fig. 27.11).
This complex spans the plasma membrane and serves as a link between
the cytoskeleton inside the myofiber and the basement membrane out-
side of the cell. By doing so, dystrophin is thought to provide mechani-
cal stability to the myofiber and its cell membrane during muscle con-
traction. Defects in the complex may lead to small membrane tears that
permit influx of calcium, triggering events that result in myofiber ne-
crosis. In addition to its mechanical function, dystrophin may have a
role in signaling pathways; for example, its carboxy terminus interacts
with nitric oxide synthase, which generates nitric oxide (NO).
Identification and characterization of pathogenic dystrophin muta-
tions has provided an explanation for some of the phenotypic variation
in patients with dystrophinopathies. Duchenne muscular dystrophy is
typically associated with deletions or frameshift mutations that result

MORPHOLOGY
The basic morphologic changes that muscular dystrophies elicit in skeletal
muscle tissue may differ in severity but are otherwise similar. The changes
in Duchenne muscular dystrophy serve as an example. This disease is
marked by chronic muscle injury that outpaces the capacity for repair
(Fig. 27.12). Muscle biopsies in young boys show ongoing damage in the
form of segmental myofiber necrosis and regeneration associated
with an admixture of atrophic myofibers. The fascicular architecture is
preserved during the earlier stages of the disease, and there is usually no
inflammation except for the presence of myophagocytosis. As the disease
progresses, muscle tissue is replaced by collagen and fat cells (“fatty re-
placement” or “fatty infiltration”). This remodeling distorts the fascicular
architecture of the muscle, which becomes markedly abnormal over time. At
later time points, the remaining myofibers show prominent variation in size
ranging from small atrophic fibers to large, hypertrophied fibers. Immunohis-
tochemical studies for dystrophin can be used to document complete or
partial absence of dystrophin in Duchenne (Fig. 27.12B) and Becker muscular
dystrophy, respectively.

• Conditions with defects in extracellular matrix surrounding myofibers. These are exemplified by Ullrich congenital muscular dystrophy (UCMD) and merosin deficiency. In the former, the causative mutations involve one of three collagen VI a genes; in the case of merosin deficiency, the gene encoding merosin (LAMA2) is disrupted. Fig. 27.12 Duchenne muscular dystrophy. Histologic images of muscle biopsy specimens from two brothers.
(A–B) Specimens from a 3-year-old boy. (A) At a younger age, fascicular muscle architecture is maintained,
but myofibers show variation in size. There is a cluster of basophilic regenerating myofibers (left side) and
slight endomysial fibrosis, seen as focal pink-staining connective tissue between myofibers. (B) Immunohistochemical staining shows complete absence of membrane-associated dystrophin, stained brown in normal
muscle (inset). (C) Biopsy specimen from the older (9-year-old) brother illustrates disease progression marked
by extensive variation in myofiber size, fatty replacement, and endomysial fibrosis.
Clinical Features
Boys with Duchenne muscular dystrophy appear normal at birth. Very
early motor milestones are met, but walking is often delayed. The first
indications of muscle weakness are clumsiness and inability to keep up
with peers. Weakness begins in the pelvic girdle muscles and then extends to the shoulder girdle. Enlargement of the muscles of the lower leg
associated with weakness, termed pseudohypertrophy, is often present.
The mean age of wheelchair dependence is around 9.5 years. Patients
develop joint contractures, scoliosis, worsening respiratory reserve, and
sleep hypoventilation as the disease continues to progress.
Dystrophin is also expressed in the heart and the CNS. Dystrophin deficiency in cardiac muscle often leads to the development of
cardiomyopathy and arrhythmias, particularly in older patients.
Cognitive impairment and learning disabilities, presumably due to a
functional role for dystrophin in the brain, are also common and
sometimes produce intellectual disability. Patients with Duchenne
muscular dystrophy often succumb to their disease before the age of
25 or 30 years because of respiratory insufficiency, pulmonary infections, and heart failure despite optimal supportive care. This contrasts with Becker muscular dystrophy, which typically presents in
later childhood, adolescence, or even adult life; has slower progression; and may allow a near-normal life expectancy. Cardiac involvement leading to heart failure is a common life-limiting complication.
The diagnosis is based on history, physical examination, and laboratory studies. Serum creatine kinase is markedly elevated during the
first decade of life due to ongoing muscle damage, and then falls as
the disease progresses and muscle mass is lost. Genetic testing provides
the ultimate confirmation of the diagnosis, but muscle biopsies can still
be helpful in cases with difficult to identify genetic alterations.
Limb-Girdle Muscular Dystrophy. Limb-girdle muscular dystrophies are a heterogeneous group of at least 8 autosomal dominant
and 23 autosomal recessive entities. Their overall incidence is 1 in
25,000 to 50,000 individuals. As indicated by the name, all forms are
characterized by muscle weakness that preferentially involves proximal muscle groups. Both age of onset and disease severity are highly
variable. The causative mutations involve genes that participate in
diverse cellular functions, making it difficult to discern a unifying
mechanism of disease pathogenesis. Based on current knowledge, the
implicated genes can be grouped according to the proteins they
encode:
• Structural components of the dystrophin glycoprotein complex such
as the sarcoglycans (Fig. 27.11)
• Enzymes that glycosylate α-dystroglycan, a component of the dystrophin glycoprotein complex (see Fig. 27.11)
• Proteins that associate with the Z-disks of sarcomeres
• Proteins involved in vesicle trafficking and cell signaling
• Proteins of seemingly diverse function such as the protease calpain
3, and lamin A/C (which is also mutated in some patients with
Emery-Dreifuss muscular dystrophy; see next)
Emery-Dreifuss Muscular Dystrophy (EMD). EMD is caused by
mutations in genes that encode nuclear lamin proteins. Clinically, it
is marked by a triad consisting of slowly progressive humeroperoneal
weakness; cardiomyopathy associated with conduction defects; and
early contractures of the Achilles tendon, spine, and elbows. The
X-linked form (EMD1) and the autosomal form (EMD2) are caused by
mutations in the genes encoding emerin and lamin A/C, respectively,
both of which localize to the inner face of the nuclear membrane. It is
hypothesized that these proteins help maintain the shape and mechanical stability of the nucleus during muscle contraction. They may
also influence gene expression by affecting chromatin organization in
the nucleus. How defects in these proteins produce the observed
phenotypes is unknown.

Fig. 27.12 Duchenne muscular dystrophy. Histologic images of muscle biopsy specimens from two brothers.
(A–B) Specimens from a 3-year-old boy. (A) At a younger age, fascicular muscle architecture is maintained,
but myofibers show variation in size. There is a cluster of basophilic regenerating myofibers (left side) and
slight endomysial fibrosis, seen as focal pink-staining connective tissue between myofibers. (B) Immunohis-
tochemical staining shows complete absence of membrane-associated dystrophin, stained brown in normal
muscle (inset). (C) Biopsy specimen from the older (9-year-old) brother illustrates disease progression marked
by extensive variation in myofiber size, fatty replacement, and endomysial fibrosis.
Clinical Features
Boys with Duchenne muscular dystrophy appear normal at birth. Very
early motor milestones are met, but walking is often delayed. The first
indications of muscle weakness are clumsiness and inability to keep up
with peers. Weakness begins in the pelvic girdle muscles and then ex-
tends to the shoulder girdle. Enlargement of the muscles of the lower leg
associated with weakness, termed pseudohypertrophy, is often present.
The mean age of wheelchair dependence is around 9.5 years. Patients
develop joint contractures, scoliosis, worsening respiratory reserve, and
sleep hypoventilation as the disease continues to progress.
Dystrophin is also expressed in the heart and the CNS. Dystro-
phin deficiency in cardiac muscle often leads to the development of
cardiomyopathy and arrhythmias, particularly in older patients.
Cognitive impairment and learning disabilities, presumably due to a
functional role for dystrophin in the brain, are also common and
sometimes produce intellectual disability. Patients with Duchenne
muscular dystrophy often succumb to their disease before the age of
25 or 30 years because of respiratory insufficiency, pulmonary infec-
tions, and heart failure despite optimal supportive care. This con-
trasts with Becker muscular dystrophy, which typically presents in
later childhood, adolescence, or even adult life; has slower progres-
sion; and may allow a near-normal life expectancy. Cardiac involve-
ment leading to heart failure is a common life-limiting complication.
The diagnosis is based on history, physical examination, and labora-
tory studies. Serum creatine kinase is markedly elevated during the
first decade of life due to ongoing muscle damage, and then falls as
the disease progresses and muscle mass is lost. Genetic testing provides
the ultimate confirmation of the diagnosis, but muscle biopsies can still
be helpful in cases with difficult to identify genetic alterations.
Limb-Girdle Muscular Dystrophy. Limb-girdle muscular dystro-
phies are a heterogeneous group of at least 8 autosomal dominant
and 23 autosomal recessive entities. Their overall incidence is 1 in
25,000 to 50,000 individuals. As indicated by the name, all forms are
characterized by muscle weakness that preferentially involves proxi-
mal muscle groups. Both age of onset and disease severity are highly
variable. The causative mutations involve genes that participate in
diverse cellular functions, making it difficult to discern a unifying
mechanism of disease pathogenesis. Based on current knowledge, the
implicated genes can be grouped according to the proteins they
encode:
• Structural components of the dystrophin glycoprotein complex such
as the sarcoglycans (Fig. 27.11)
• Enzymes that glycosylate a-dystroglycan, a component of the dys-
trophin glycoprotein complex (see Fig. 27.11)
• Proteins that associate with the Z-disks of sarcomeres
• Proteins involved in vesicle trafficking and cell signaling
• Proteins of seemingly diverse function such as the protease calpain
3, and lamin A/C (which is also mutated in some patients with
Emery-Dreifuss muscular dystrophy; see next)
Emery-Dreifuss Muscular Dystrophy (EMD). EMD is caused by
mutations in genes that encode nuclear lamin proteins. Clinically, it
is marked by a triad consisting of slowly progressive humeroperoneal
weakness; cardiomyopathy associated with conduction defects; and
early contractures of the Achilles tendon, spine, and elbows. The
X-linked form (EMD1) and the autosomal form (EMD2) are caused by
mutations in the genes encoding emerin and lamin A/C, respectively,
both of which localize to the inner face of the nuclear membrane. It is
hypothesized that these proteins help maintain the shape and me-
chanical stability of the nucleus during muscle contraction. They may
also influence gene expression by affecting chromatin organization in
the nucleus. How defects in these proteins produce the observed
phenotypes is unknown.

CHAPTER 27 Peripheral Nerves and Skeletal Muscles 1123
Facioscapulohumeral Dystrophy. Facioscapulohumeral dystrophy is associated with a characteristic pattern of muscle involvement that includes prominent weakness of facial muscles and muscles of the shoulder girdle. It is an autosomal dominant disease
affecting about 1 in 20,000 individuals.
Pathogenesis
The pathogenesis of facioscapulohumeral dystrophy is complex and
unique. The disease is linked to epigenetic derepression of the gene
encoding the transcription factor DUX4, which is silenced in most
somatic tissues and can be toxic in cells such as myofibers. In most
cases the derepression is thought to result from mutations in regulatory sequences that lead to altered DNA methylation, chromatin relaxation, and DUX4 transcription in skeletal muscle. In a small proportion of cases the derepression of DUX4 results from mutations in
chromatin repressors such as SMCHD1.
Ion Channel Myopathies (Channelopathies)
Channelopathies are a group of inherited diseases caused by
mutations affecting the function of ion channel proteins. Most
channelopathies are autosomal dominant disorders with variable
penetrance. Depending on the channel that is affected, clinical
manifestations may include epilepsy, migraine, movement disorders
with cerebellar dysfunction, peripheral nerve disease, and muscle
disease. The following discussion focuses on those channelopathies
with muscle involvement.
Myotonic Dystrophy. Myotonic dystrophy is an autosomal dominant multisystem disorder associated with skeletal muscle weakness, cataracts, endocrinopathy, and cardiomyopathy. It affects
about 1 in 10,000 individuals. Myotonia, a sustained involuntary contraction of muscles, is a key feature of this disease, which can be variably classified with muscular dystrophies or channelopathies based on
its unique pathogenesis.
Pathogenesis
Myotonic dystrophy is a trinucleotide repeat expansion disease that
results from CTG expansion in the DMPK gene (type 1, DM1) or
CCTG expansions in the CNBP gene (type 2, DM2). The following
discussion focuses on the more common DM1 variant. The correlation between the length of expansion and disease severity is not as
strong as in some other triplet repeat expansion disorders like
Huntington disease (Chapter 28) but severe congenital myotonic dystrophy is typically linked to larger repeat sizes. Experimental studies
suggest that the skeletal muscle phenotype stems from a “toxic” gain-of-function caused by the triplet repeat expansion. Specifically, the
expanded CTG-repeats in the DMPK mRNA transcript appear to
bind and sequester muscle splicing regulators. This, in turn, is thought
to lead to alternative splicing of several genes including CLCN1,
which encodes a chloride channel. It is believed that the resulting
deficiency of this chloride channel is responsible for the myotonia; of
note in this regard, mutations in CLCN1 itself are linked to congenital
myotonia. Insulin resistance and diabetes in DM1 may be the result of
alternate splicing of insulin receptor isoforms in skeletal muscle.
Differential expression of other genes and accumulation of transcripts
containing the trinucleotide repeat may contribute to other manifestations of this disease.
Other Ion Channel Myopathies. Different ion channel myopathies
may cause decreased or increased excitability resulting in hypotonia
or hypertonia. Disorders associated with hypotonia can be further
subclassified based on whether symptomatic patients have elevated,
depressed, or normal serum potassium levels and are called hyperkale-mic, hypokalemic, or normokalemic periodic paralysis, respectively.
Examples of genes that when mutated lead to periodic paralysis or
related disorders include the following:
• KCNJ2: Mutations affecting this potassium channel cause Andersen-
Tawil syndrome, an autosomal disorder associated with periodic
paralysis, cardiac arrhythmias, and skeletal abnormalities.
• SCN4A: Mutations affecting this sodium channel cause several autosomal disorders with presentations ranging from myotonia to
periodic paralysis.
• CACNA1S: Missense mutations in this protein, a subunit of a
muscle calcium channel, are the most common cause of hypokalemic paralysis.
• CLCN1: Mutations affecting this chloride channel cause myotonia
congenita. As already discussed, CLCN1 expression is decreased in
myotonic dystrophy.
• RYR1: Mutations in the RYR1 gene disrupt the function of the
ryanodine receptor, which regulates calcium release from the sarcoplasmic reticulum. RYR1 mutations are linked to a congenital
myopathy (central core disease) and to malignant hyperthermia.
The latter is characterized by a hypermetabolic state (tachycardia,
tachypnea, muscle spasms, and later hyperpyrexia) that can be triggered by anesthetics, most commonly halogenated inhalational
agents and succinylcholine. Upon exposure to anesthetic, the mutated receptor allows increased efflux of calcium from the sarcoplasmic reticulum, leading to tetany and excessive heat production.
Diseases of Lipid or Glycogen Metabolism
Many inborn errors of lipid or glycogen metabolism affect skeletal
muscle. These disorders tend to produce one of two general patterns of
muscle dysfunction. Some lead to patients presenting with episodic
symptoms that are brought on by events like fasting or exercise and can
include muscle cramping, pain, or rhabdomyolysis from extensive
muscle necrosis. Other metabolic myopathies result in slowly progressive damage akin to a dystrophy without episodic manifestations.
Listed here are some examples:
• Carnitine palmitoyltransferase II deficiency is the most common
disorder of lipid metabolism to cause episodic muscle damage with
exercise or fasting. The defect in this disorder impairs the transport
of free fatty acids into mitochondria.
• Myophosphorylase deficiency (McArdle disease) is one of the more
common glycogen storage diseases affecting skeletal muscle; it also
results in episodic muscle damage with exercise.
• Acid maltase deficiency results in impaired lysosomal metabolism
of glycogen, glycogen aggregation, and disruption of lysosomal

Facioscapulohumeral Dystrophy. Facioscapulohumeral dystro-
phy is associated with a characteristic pattern of muscle involve-
ment that includes prominent weakness of facial muscles and mus-
cles of the shoulder girdle. It is an autosomal dominant disease
affecting about 1 in 20,000 individuals.
Pathogenesis
The pathogenesis of facioscapulohumeral dystrophy is complex and
unique. The disease is linked to epigenetic derepression of the gene
encoding the transcription factor DUX4, which is silenced in most
somatic tissues and can be toxic in cells such as myofibers. In most
cases the derepression is thought to result from mutations in regula-
tory sequences that lead to altered DNA methylation, chromatin relax-
ation, and DUX4 transcription in skeletal muscle. In a small propor-
tion of cases the derepression of DUX4 results from mutations in
chromatin repressors such as SMCHD1.
Ion Channel Myopathies (Channelopathies)
Channelopathies are a group of inherited diseases caused by
mutations affecting the function of ion channel proteins. Most
channelopathies are autosomal dominant disorders with variable
penetrance. Depending on the channel that is affected, clinical
manifestations may include epilepsy, migraine, movement disorders
with cerebellar dysfunction, peripheral nerve disease, and muscle
disease. The following discussion focuses on those channelopathies
with muscle involvement.
Myotonic Dystrophy. Myotonic dystrophy is an autosomal domi-
nant multisystem disorder associated with skeletal muscle weak-
ness, cataracts, endocrinopathy, and cardiomyopathy. It affects
about 1 in 10,000 individuals. Myotonia, a sustained involuntary con-
traction of muscles, is a key feature of this disease, which can be vari-
ably classified with muscular dystrophies or channelopathies based on
its unique pathogenesis.
Pathogenesis
Myotonic dystrophy is a trinucleotide repeat expansion disease that
results from CTG expansion in the DMPK gene (type 1, DM1) or
CCTG expansions in the CNBP gene (type 2, DM2). The following
discussion focuses on the more common DM1 variant. The correla-
tion between the length of expansion and disease severity is not as
strong as in some other triplet repeat expansion disorders like
Huntington disease (Chapter 28) but severe congenital myotonic dys-
trophy is typically linked to larger repeat sizes. Experimental studies
suggest that the skeletal muscle phenotype stems from a “toxic” gain-
of-function caused by the triplet repeat expansion. Specifically, the
expanded CTG-repeats in the DMPK mRNA transcript appear to
bind and sequester muscle splicing regulators. This, in turn, is thought
to lead to alternative splicing of several genes including CLCN1,
which encodes a chloride channel. It is believed that the resulting
deficiency of this chloride channel is responsible for the myotonia; of
note in this regard, mutations in CLCN1 itself are linked to congenital
myotonia. Insulin resistance and diabetes in DM1 may be the result of
alternate splicing of insulin receptor isoforms in skeletal muscle.
Differential expression of other genes and accumulation of transcripts
containing the trinucleotide repeat may contribute to other manifes-
tations of this disease.
Other Ion Channel Myopathies. Different ion channel myopathies
may cause decreased or increased excitability resulting in hypotonia
or hypertonia. Disorders associated with hypotonia can be further
subclassified based on whether symptomatic patients have elevated,
depressed, or normal serum potassium levels and are called hyperkale-
mic, hypokalemic, or normokalemic periodic paralysis, respectively.
Examples of genes that when mutated lead to periodic paralysis or
related disorders include the following:
• KCNJ2: Mutations affecting this potassium channel cause Andersen-
Tawil syndrome, an autosomal disorder associated with periodic
paralysis, cardiac arrhythmias, and skeletal abnormalities.
• SCN4A: Mutations affecting this sodium channel cause several au-
tosomal disorders with presentations ranging from myotonia to
periodic paralysis.
• CACNA1S: Missense mutations in this protein, a subunit of a
muscle calcium channel, are the most common cause of hypokale-
mic paralysis.
• CLCN1: Mutations affecting this chloride channel cause myotonia
congenita. As already discussed, CLCN1 expression is decreased in
myotonic dystrophy.
• RYR1: Mutations in the RYR1 gene disrupt the function of the
ryanodine receptor, which regulates calcium release from the sar-
coplasmic reticulum. RYR1 mutations are linked to a congenital
myopathy (central core disease) and to malignant hyperthermia.
The latter is characterized by a hypermetabolic state (tachycardia,
tachypnea, muscle spasms, and later hyperpyrexia) that can be trig-
gered by anesthetics, most commonly halogenated inhalational
agents and succinylcholine. Upon exposure to anesthetic, the mu-
tated receptor allows increased efflux of calcium from the sarco-
plasmic reticulum, leading to tetany and excessive heat production.

Many inborn errors of lipid or glycogen metabolism affect skeletal
muscle. These disorders tend to produce one of two general patterns of
muscle dysfunction. Some lead to patients presenting with episodic
symptoms that are brought on by events like fasting or exercise and can
include muscle cramping, pain, or rhabdomyolysis from extensive
muscle necrosis. Other metabolic myopathies result in slowly progres-
sive damage akin to a dystrophy without episodic manifestations.

ongoing for possible gene replacement therapy.

KEY CONCEPTS
Disorders of Skeletal Muscle
• Altered muscle function may stem from neurogenic or primary myopathic
processes.
• Myopathic disorders are often marked by necrosis and regeneration of
myofibers.
• Inflammatory myopathies are often linked to distinct autoantibodies, clinical
presentation, and histopathologic changes and include dermatomyositis
(DM), antisynthetase syndrome, immune-mediated necrotizing myopathy
(IMNM), sporadic inclusion body myositis (sIBM), as well as overlap myositis. This classification has largely replaced the traditional triad of polymyositis, dermatomyositis, and inclusion body myositis.
• DM occurs in children and adults. Distinct clinical subtypes are associated
with specific autoantibodies. DM can be a paraneoplastic disease in adults.
A hallmark feature not found in all cases is perifascicular atrophy.
• Antisynthetase syndrome is associated with distinct antibodies, most often
anti-Jo1, and necrotizing changes in a perifascicular distribution.
• IMNM is associated with HMGCR or SRP antibodies, is associated with
muscle necrosis, and often lacks prominent inflammatory cell infiltrates.
• sIBM is a chronic, progressive disease of older patients associated with
rimmed vacuoles.
• Muscular dystrophies and congenital myopathies result from genetic mutations that disrupt the function of proteins that are important for various
aspects of muscle development, function, and regeneration. Some of these
diseases present in infancy, others in adulthood. They may be relentlessly
progressive or cause relatively static deficits.
• Myopathy can result from toxic injury or be the result of metabolic diseases including those of lipid metabolism, glycogen metabolism, and
mitochondria.
PERIPHERAL NERVE SHEATH TUMORS
Most benign and malignant neoplasms of peripheral nerve sheaths
are composed of cells that show evidence of Schwann cell differentiation. These include three common types: schwannoma, neurofibroma, and malignant peripheral nerve sheath tumor (MPNST).
Peripheral nerve sheath tumors have several unique features. First,
they are associated with relatively common familial tumor syndromes,
including neurofibromatosis type 1 (NF1), neurofibromatosis type 2
(NF2), and schwannomatosis. Second, MPNSTs seen in the context of
NF1 are thought to arise through malignant transformation of preexisting neurofibromas. Malignant transformation of a preexisting
benign lesion is a common origin for certain carcinomas (e.g., colon
cancer) but is unusual in soft tissue tumors.
Neurofibromatosis
Neurofibromatosis Type 1
This is a common autosomal dominant disorder with a frequency of 1
in 3000 individuals. It is a systemic disease associated with nonneoplastic manifestations and with a variety of tumors, including neurofibromas, MPNSTs, gliomas of the optic nerve, other gliomas
(Chapter  28), and pheochromocytomas. Other features include
intellectual disability, seizures, skeletal defects, pigmented nodules of
the iris (Lisch nodules), and cutaneous hyperpigmented macules (café
au lait spots). The disease is caused by loss-of-function mutations in
the NF1 gene, located at 17q11.2, which encodes the tumor suppressor
neurofibromin. The neoplastic cells in NF1-related tumors lack neurofibromin due to biallelic defects of the NF1 gene. As discussed in
Chapter 7, NF1 protein has GTPase activity that restrains RAS function. In the absence of NF1, RAS remains trapped in its active state.
The disease has a high penetrance but variable expressivity. Some
patients exhibit only subtle features, while others show disease that is
restricted to certain parts of the body, a distribution that is attributable
to mosaicism. An unfortunate subset has severe disease. Large chromosomal deletions that span NF1 and extend to involve adjacent genes
tend to be associated with more severe phenotypes.
Neurofibromatosis Type 2
This is an autosomal dominant disorder associated with the development of schwannomas, meningiomas, and spinal ependymomas (but
not neurofibromas). Bilateral vestibular schwannomas are a hallmark
of this disease and are found in many affected patients. This disorder is
less common than NF1, having a frequency of 1 in 40,000 to 50,000
individuals. Certain other rare familial syndromes are also associated
with multiple schwannomas, such as schwannomatosis.
The NF2 gene is located on chromosome 22q12 and is also commonly mutated in sporadic spinal ependymomas, meningiomas and
schwannomas. The NF2 gene product, merlin, is a cytoskeletal protein
that participates in the regulation of several key signaling pathways
that are involved in control of cell shape, cell growth, and cell adhesion.
There is some correlation between the type of mutation and clinical
symptoms, with nonsense and frameshift mutations causing more
severe phenotypes than missense mutations.
Schwannomas
These are benign tumors that exhibit Schwann cell differentiation
and arise from peripheral nerves. Schwannomas are a component of
NF2, and even sporadic schwannomas are commonly associated with
somatic inactivating mutations in the NF2 gene.
MORPHOLOGY
Schwannomas are well-circumscribed, encapsulated masses that attach loosely
to the associated nerve without invading it. Grossly, these tumors form firm,
gray masses. Microscopically, they are composed of Schwann cells that typically have a spindled elongated nucleus with a wavy or buckled shape. Like
normal Schwann cells, the tumor cells express the markers S100 and SOX10
and are surrounded by continuous basement membrane that can be visualized
by electron microscopy or immunohistochemistry. Schwannomas typically include regions referred to as Antoni A areas in which the cells are arranged in
distinct patterns like streaming fascicles and other areas referred to as Antoni
B areas that appear more myxoid and exhibit less distinct architectural patterning (Fig. 27.14A). Palisading of nuclei is common in the Antoni A areas and arrangements with palisading nuclei around central “nuclear-free zones” are
termed Verocay bodies (Fig. 27.14B). A variety of degenerative changes may
be found in schwannomas, including nuclear pleomorphism, xanthomatous
change, vascular hyalinization, cystic change, and necrosis. Some large, mitotically active schwannomas lacking Antoni B areas can mimic a sarcoma.
Clinical Features
Schwann cells are present around the axons in cranial nerves II
through XII, nerve roots, large named nerves as well as tiny, distal
nerve branches, and schwannomas can occur in all these locations. The

Disorders of Skeletal Muscle

• Myopathic disorders are often marked by necrosis and regeneration of myofibers.

• IMNM is associated with HMGCR or SRP antibodies, is associated with muscle necrosis, and often lacks prominent inflammatory cell infiltrates.

• sIBM is a chronic, progressive disease of older patients associated with rimmed vacuoles.

• Muscular dystrophies and congenital myopathies result from genetic mutations that disrupt the function of proteins that are important for various aspects of muscle development, function, and regeneration. Some of these diseases present in infancy, others in adulthood. They may be relentlessly progressive or cause relatively static deficits.

Neurofibromas
Neurofibromas are benign nerve sheath tumors that are more heterogeneous in composition than schwannomas. The neoplastic Schwann
cells are admixed with perineurial-like cells, fibroblasts, mast cells,
and CD341 spindle cells. Neurofibromas may be either sporadic or
NF1-associated. Different types of neurofibroma can be distinguished
depending on their growth pattern.
• Superficial cutaneous neurofibromas often present as pedunculated
nodules that can be seen isolated (if sporadic) or multiple (if NF1-
associated).
• Diffuse neurofibromas often present as a large plaque-like elevation
of skin and are typically NF1-associated.
• Plexiform neurofibromas can be found in deep or superficial locations
in association with nerve roots or large nerves and are uniformly
NF1-associated.
Pathogenesis
Only the Schwann cells in neurofibromas show complete loss of the
NF1 gene product, neurofibromin, indicating that these are neoplastic
cells. Haploinsufficiency for the NF1 gene in other associated cells may
also contribute to the growth of NF1-associated tumors. For example,
there is evidence that NF1-haploinsufficient mast cells are hypersensitive to KIT ligand produced by Schwann cells and in response secrete
factors that stimulate Schwann cell growth. This form of tumor/stromal
cell cross-talk may be targetable with inhibitors of the KIT receptor
tyrosine kinase. Other studies suggest that plexiform neurofibromas
and dermal neurofibromas arise from different neural crest–derived
precursor cells. Malignant transformation of neurofibroma to MPNST
is usually observed in the plexiform variant but is sometimes also seen

CHAPTER 27 Peripheral Nerves and Skeletal Muscles 1127
in the diffuse type. The overall incidence of MPNST in NF1 patients is
about 5% to 10%, but patients with large numbers of plexiform neurofibromas and large deletions in the NF1 gene are at higher risk.
MORPHOLOGY
Localized cutaneous neurofibroma. These are small, well-delineated but
unencapsulated nodular lesions that arise in the dermis and subcutaneous fat.
They have relatively low cellularity and contain bland Schwann cells admixed
with stromal cells such as mast cells, perineurial cells, CD341 spindle cells,
and fibroblasts. Adnexal structures are sometimes entrapped at the edges of
the lesion. The stroma of these tumors contains loose collagen.
Diffuse neurofibroma. This tumor has morphologic features similar to
those seen in localized cutaneous neurofibromas but exhibits a distinctly different growth pattern. The tumor diffusely infiltrates dermis, subcutaneous
connective tissue, or deep soft tissues, entrapping fat and appendage structures, resulting in large, often plaque-like, lesions. Focal collections of cells
mimicking the appearance of Meissner corpuscles (so-called pseudo-
Meissner corpuscles or tactile-like bodies) are an associated feature.
Plexiform neurofibroma. These tumors grow within and expand multiple
nerve fascicles (Fig. 27.14C), entrapping associated axons. The external perineurial layer of the nerve is preserved, giving individual nodules an encapsulated appearance. The expanded, ropy thickening of multiple nerve fascicles
results in what is sometimes referred to as a “bag of worms” appearance upon
gross examination. The tumor has a cellular composition similar to that of
other neurofibromas. The extracellular matrix varies from loose and myxoid to
more collagenous and fibrous. Collagen is often seen in bundles likened to
“shredded carrots” (Fig. 27.14D).
Malignant Peripheral Nerve Sheath Tumors
Most malignant peripheral nerve sheath tumors (MPNSTs) are high-grade tumors, but low-grade variants are recognized. About half arise
in NF1 patients and are assumed to result from malignant transformation of a plexiform neurofibroma. Sporadic cases may arise de novo.
Most are associated with larger peripheral nerves in the chest, abdomen, pelvis, neck, or limb-girdle. MPNSTs exhibit complex chromosomal aberrations including chromosome gains and losses. High-grade
MPNSTs exhibit genetic or epigenetic abnormalities in addition to
NF1 alterations. These include loss of the polycomb repressor complex
PRC2, which is responsible for placing repression marks on histone H3;
and trimethylated histone 3; homozygous loss of CDKN2A/B, which
encodes several tumor suppressor proteins, including the cell cycle
regulator p16 and the p53 regulator p14.
MORPHOLOGY
The lesions are poorly defined tumor masses that infiltrate along the axis of the
parent nerve and invade adjacent soft tissues. A wide range of histologic appearances can be encountered. Typical cases show a fasciculated arrangement
of spindle cells. At low power the tumor often appears “marbleized” due to
variations in cellularity. Mitoses, necrosis, and nuclear anaplasia are common.
An interesting phenomenon observed in MPNST is described as “divergent
differentiation.” This term refers to the presence of focal areas that exhibit
other lines of differentiation, including glandular, cartilaginous, osseous, or
rhabdomyoblastic morphology. A tumor exhibiting the latter is referred to as
Triton tumor. Due to the poorly differentiated nature of MPNST, the distinction from an undifferentiated sarcoma may not be straightforward. Helpful
clues include a diagnosis of NF1 in the affected patient, a clearly demonstrated anatomic relationship to a nerve or to a preexisting neurofibroma, and
the presence of molecular changes described above.
Other Types of Nerve Sheath Tumors
There are other tumors that are thought to be derived from Schwann
cells or perineurial cells.
• Malignant melanotic nerve sheath tumor (MMNST) was formerly
referred to as “melanotic schwannoma” but is driven by distinctly
different genetic changes, particularly PRKAR1A mutations that
lead to increased cAMP-dependent signaling. MMNSTs can be associated with Carney complex and are clinically more aggressive
than schwannomas.
• Granular cell tumor is composed of polygonal cells filled with lysosomes resulting in the appearance of distinctly granular cytoplasm.
Most of these form small superficial or mucosal masses. These tumors are associated with genetic changes in genes affecting vacuolar
ATPase function.
• Perineurioma is a soft tissue lesion that is thought to arise from the
perineurial cells that normally surround individual nerve fascicles.
KEY CONCEPTS
Peripheral Nerve Sheath Tumors
• The three common peripheral nerve sheath tumors—schwannoma, neurofibroma, and MPNST—all arise from cells of Schwann cell lineage.
• Schwannomas are encapsulated benign tumors that can be associated
with NF2.
• Neurofibromas are benign peripheral nerve sheath tumors sometimes
associated with NF1 that can be subtyped as localized cutaneous, diffuse,
or plexiform.
• MPNSTs can be de novo sporadic neoplasms or NF1-associated tumors
arising through malignant transformation of a (plexiform) neurofibroma.

in the diffuse type. The overall incidence of MPNST in NF1 patients is
about 5% to 10%, but patients with large numbers of plexiform neuro-
fibromas and large deletions in the NF1 gene are at higher risk.
MORPHOLOGY
Localized cutaneous neurofibroma. These are small, well-delineated but
unencapsulated nodular lesions that arise in the dermis and subcutaneous fat.
They have relatively low cellularity and contain bland Schwann cells admixed
with stromal cells such as mast cells, perineurial cells, CD341 spindle cells,
and fibroblasts. Adnexal structures are sometimes entrapped at the edges of
the lesion. The stroma of these tumors contains loose collagen.
Diffuse neurofibroma. This tumor has morphologic features similar to
those seen in localized cutaneous neurofibromas but exhibits a distinctly dif-
ferent growth pattern. The tumor diffusely infiltrates dermis, subcutaneous
connective tissue, or deep soft tissues, entrapping fat and appendage struc-
tures, resulting in large, often plaque-like, lesions. Focal collections of cells
mimicking the appearance of Meissner corpuscles (so-called pseudo-
Meissner corpuscles or tactile-like bodies) are an associated feature.
Plexiform neurofibroma. These tumors grow within and expand multiple
nerve fascicles (Fig. 27.14C), entrapping associated axons. The external peri-
neurial layer of the nerve is preserved, giving individual nodules an encapsu-
lated appearance. The expanded, ropy thickening of multiple nerve fascicles
results in what is sometimes referred to as a “bag of worms” appearance upon
gross examination. The tumor has a cellular composition similar to that of
other neurofibromas. The extracellular matrix varies from loose and myxoid to
more collagenous and fibrous. Collagen is often seen in bundles likened to
“shredded carrots” (Fig. 27.14D).
Malignant Peripheral Nerve Sheath Tumors
Most malignant peripheral nerve sheath tumors (MPNSTs) are high-
grade tumors, but low-grade variants are recognized. About half arise
in NF1 patients and are assumed to result from malignant transforma-
tion of a plexiform neurofibroma. Sporadic cases may arise de novo.
Most are associated with larger peripheral nerves in the chest, abdo-
men, pelvis, neck, or limb-girdle. MPNSTs exhibit complex chromo-
somal aberrations including chromosome gains and losses. High-grade
MPNSTs exhibit genetic or epigenetic abnormalities in addition to
NF1 alterations. These include loss of the polycomb repressor complex
PRC2, which is responsible for placing repression marks on histone H3;
and trimethylated histone 3; homozygous loss of CDKN2A/B, which
encodes several tumor suppressor proteins, including the cell cycle
regulator p16 and the p53 regulator p14.
MORPHOLOGY
The lesions are poorly defined tumor masses that infiltrate along the axis of the
parent nerve and invade adjacent soft tissues. A wide range of histologic ap-
pearances can be encountered. Typical cases show a fasciculated arrangement
of spindle cells. At low power the tumor often appears “marbleized” due to
variations in cellularity. Mitoses, necrosis, and nuclear anaplasia are common.
An interesting phenomenon observed in MPNST is described as “divergent
differentiation.” This term refers to the presence of focal areas that exhibit
other lines of differentiation, including glandular, cartilaginous, osseous, or
rhabdomyoblastic morphology. A tumor exhibiting the latter is referred to as
Triton tumor. Due to the poorly differentiated nature of MPNST, the distinc-
tion from an undifferentiated sarcoma may not be straightforward. Helpful
clues include a diagnosis of NF1 in the affected patient, a clearly demon-
strated anatomic relationship to a nerve or to a preexisting neurofibroma, and
the presence of molecular changes described above.
Other Types of Nerve Sheath Tumors
There are other tumors that are thought to be derived from Schwann
cells or perineurial cells.
• Malignant melanotic nerve sheath tumor (MMNST) was formerly
referred to as “melanotic schwannoma” but is driven by distinctly
different genetic changes, particularly PRKAR1A mutations that
lead to increased cAMP-dependent signaling. MMNSTs can be as-
sociated with Carney complex and are clinically more aggressive
than schwannomas.
• Granular cell tumor is composed of polygonal cells filled with lyso-
somes resulting in the appearance of distinctly granular cytoplasm.
Most of these form small superficial or mucosal masses. These tu-
mors are associated with genetic changes in genes affecting vacuolar
ATPase function.
• Perineurioma is a soft tissue lesion that is thought to arise from the
perineurial cells that normally surround individual nerve fascicles.
KEY CONCEPTS
Peripheral Nerve Sheath Tumors
• The three common peripheral nerve sheath tumors—schwannoma, neurofi-
broma, and MPNST—all arise from cells of Schwann cell lineage.
• Schwannomas are encapsulated benign tumors that can be associated
with NF2.
• Neurofibromas are benign peripheral nerve sheath tumors sometimes
associated with NF1 that can be subtyped as localized cutaneous, diffuse,
or plexiform.
• MPNSTs can be de novo sporadic neoplasms or NF1-associated tumors
arising through malignant transformation of a (plexiform) neurofibroma.
